content: Neglected diseases are a group of tropical infections that predominantly affect low-income populations in developing regions of Africa, Asia, and the Americas. These diseases collectively cause between 500,000 and 1 million deaths annually and impose a global disease burden comparable to that of HIV/AIDS. Unlike the big three diseases—HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, and malaria—neglected diseases receive significantly less media attention and research funding. In certain cases, treatments are relatively inexpensive; for instance, the annual cost of treating schistosomiasis in children is only $0.20 per child. Trypanosomal Parasites Kala-azar (Visceral Leishmaniasis): This severe form of leishmaniasis has existing treatments, and vaccines were under development as of 2006. African Sleeping Sickness (African Trypanosomiasis): This disease, transmitted by the bite of the tsetse fly, was nearly eradicated in the 20th century. While treatments exist, they are highly toxic, and resistance to these treatments is increasing. If left untreated, the disease is invariably fatal. Chagas Disease (American Trypanosomiasis): There is no vaccine for Chagas disease. Treatments for early infection exist but are not cost-effective and are not officially approved for this purpose. Current drugs have severe side effects. Unlike other diseases, Chagas does not kill rapidly but instead causes years of debilitating chronic symptoms. The disease is transmitted through bites from South American assassin bugs. Some historians speculate that Charles Darwin may have contracted Chagas disease during his voyage on the HMS Beagle. Worm (Helminth) Parasites Schistosomiasis: This disease can be treated with the inexpensive drug praziquantel, but reinfection remains a significant issue. Other treatments are less accessible in developing regions. Multiple vaccines are under development. Schistosomiasis is caused by Schistosoma species, which have a complex life cycle involving humans and freshwater snails. Infection occurs through contact with contaminated water. The disease's pathology is unique in that the damage is caused not by the worms themselves but by the large number of eggs they produce. Lymphatic Filariasis (Elephantiasis): Antihelminthic treatments are under investigation for this condition. Onchocerciasis (River Blindness): Antihelminthic treatments are available, and prevention efforts focus on insect control. Dracunculiasis (Guinea Worm Disease): Efforts to eradicate this disease aimed for completion by 2009, as of 2007. Soil-Transmitted Helminthiases: Ascariasis (Roundworm): Antihelminthic treatments are available, and prevention involves improving food and sewage sanitation. Trichuriasis (Whipworm): Antihelminthic treatments are available, and prevention involves improving food and sewage sanitation. Hookworm: Antihelminthic treatments are available, and prevention involves improving food and sewage sanitation. Bacterial Infections Leprosy: Antibiotic treatments are available for this disease. Buruli Ulcer: Treatment involves a combination of surgical and antibiotic interventions. Trachoma: Antibiotic treatments are available, and prevention focuses on maintaining interpersonal hygiene. Cholera: Cholera is caused by the bacterium Vibrio cholerae, which contaminates drinking water. The disease manifests as severe, watery diarrhea after an incubation period of zero to five days. Cholera is particularly dangerous because it can cause death within 24 hours due to rapid dehydration. While antibacterial treatments can cure the disease, the most effective intervention is isotonic fluid replacement therapy, which reduces the mortality rate to 1%. Viral Infections Yellow Fever: A vaccine is available for yellow fever, which is caused by a flavivirus. Dengue Fever: Dengue fever, also caused by a flavivirus, is transmitted through the bite of the Aedes aegypti mosquito. While the disease is not usually fatal, infection with one of the four serotypes increases susceptibility to other serotypes, potentially leading to the life-threatening condition known as dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF). No specific treatment exists for either form of the disease beyond palliative care. Japanese Encephalitis: This disease, also caused by a flavivirus, is transmitted by Culex tritaeniorhynchus mosquitoes.
